items.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
items.summary: On Friday, November 21, 2026, secure messaging app Signal announced it is restricting users' ability to take screenshots on mobile devices. Signal President Meredith Whittaker described the move as a response to the existential threat posed by operating syste…
items.fullStory:
On Friday, November 21, 2026, secure messaging app Signal announced it is restricting users' ability to take screenshots on mobile devices. Signal President Meredith Whittaker described the move as a response to the existential threat posed by operating systems integrating agentic AI. Whittaker explained that operating systems like Windows, Android, macOS, and iOS give AI agents the ability to scan on-screen information, which undermines Signal's ability to guarantee privacy.

Whittaker stated that sensitive user data is captured, stored, and made accessible to local databases or remote servers used by OS-level AI agents, all outside of Signal's control. Previously, Signal blocked screenshots by default on its Windows app, and it is now adding similar restrictions to Android and iOS. However, users retain the option to disable this setting if they choose.

Whittaker admitted that disabling the setting would break Signal's privacy guarantees and conceded that the new restriction is an incomplete solution. She noted that the measure does not address other ways AI agents could potentially access application data.
items.whyItMatters: This news matters because the integration of OS-level AI agents capable of screen-scanning directly conflicts with the privacy guarantees of end-to-end encrypted messaging apps like Signal. It highlights a growing tension between operating system AI features and user data confidentiality.
items.whoIsAffected: Signal mobile users on Android and iOS.

Critics estimate that roughly 20% of Nvidia's business may be tied to China through indirect sales in Southeast Asia, raising questions about potential impacts on the company's bottom line. These platforms utilize various monetization strategies, ranging from free beta periods and ad-hoc subscriptions to enterprise pricing tiers. items.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
items.summary: Microdrama startup Shortical has premiered its first fully AI-generated series, titled "Inevitable," in Los Angeles. Founded in January, the company makes money primarily through subscriptions, offering bite-sized, two-minute melodramatic episodes. The new pr…
items.fullStory:
Microdrama startup Shortical has premiered its first fully AI-generated series, titled "Inevitable," in Los Angeles. Founded in January, the company makes money primarily through subscriptions, offering bite-sized, two-minute melodramatic episodes. The new project stars Israeli film and television actor Aki Avni, who licensed his face to Shortical to create a digital avatar of himself for the entirely AI-produced show. In the series, Avni plays a meta version of himself who licenses his face to a film studio before thriller-like antics ensue. According to Shortical CEO Guy Shimoni, the company is turning to AI because production overhead is substantially lower and profit potential is higher, enabling smaller teams to produce epic fantasies with kingdoms, dragons, and superheroes that were previously limited by mobile-first live-action budgets.

While China boasts the largest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni states that most of Shortical's viewers are in the U.S., skewing heavily female and frequently watching to wind down at night. Following this launch, Shortical is advertising a "LICENSE YOUR FACE" initiative on its website, where interested individuals can submit their social media handles for potential persona-contract consideration. A company representative noted that while the Avni project was done through a direct agreement, the broader platform offering is still in its early days and has not yet resulted in signed contracts. In international markets like China, face-licensing has already gained traction, with firms reportedly paying creators between $15 and $700 for their facial likenesses. Shortical has not publicly disclosed the exact financial terms of Avni's contract, though a representative stated he came on as a project partner with compensation aligning with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.

The push toward automation has unsettled many creatives and industry observers. Jennifer Cooper, founder of consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, stated that many in the industry feel impacted or have lost work to AI, turning a growing sector that provided early career opportunities for young people into a decimated landscape. Questions of consent and stolen likenesses have also dogged the industry. To manage payouts for its evolving creator base, Shortical recently partnered with Payouts.com, a platform powering gig economy disbursements at scale. Cooper suggests the broader shift is heavily driven by financial trends, noting that venture capital investors heavily favor startups mentioning AI, though she remains skeptical about whether there is genuine audience demand for AI-driven content.
items.whyItMatters: The adoption of facial licensing by startups like Shortical signals a shift toward AI-generated entertainment that could disrupt traditional actor roles and lower production costs in Hollywood. However, it also raises concerns about consent, the gig-ification of creative work, and resistance from industry professionals.
items.whoIsAffected: Actors, creators, microdrama production teams, and entertainment industry workers.

items.fullStory:

Nardelli brings extensive experience from roles at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge, and most recently served as head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion.

According to sources familiar with his thinking, Nardelli departed from Pacific Fusion's heavy reliance on physical devices for testing and simulations, believing instead that fusion startups should prioritize simulation- and data-heavy approaches. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion, which uses massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until atoms fuse and release energy.

Fusion power aims to become a significant, carbon-free energy source with nearly limitless fuel supplies, though no plant has yet supplied electricity to the commercial grid. Nardelli's pivot from AI to climate technology was driven by the potential for fusion to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change and to address AI's growing energy consumption concerns. On his website, Nardelli stated his background is in electronics and control engineering, noting that it is time to fix climate change for good.

items.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too
items.summary: On November 20, 2026, mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge announced that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis, one of the Millennium Prize math problems that conjectures a hidden structure underlying pr…
items.fullStory:
On November 20, 2026, mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge announced that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis, one of the Millennium Prize math problems that conjectures a hidden structure underlying prime numbers. Alpöge messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei the previous Sunday night to ask how to release his findings, describing a process of finding the pieces of the argument through confusion with the Claude AI model and calling the experience a "stream-of-consciousness jaunt." He and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations.

The mathematics community has begun examining the proofs in chats on Zulip, with experts like University of East Anglia number theorist Chris Birkbeck noting that the cohomology bound is proved using an automorphy-lifting argument involving Galois representations and other complex mathematical frameworks. Alpöge acknowledged that the proof currently lacks a truly human-intelligible explanation and noted it will take time for the math community to fully understand and verify the result, though the formalized Lean result is expected to hold.

Concurrently, Stanford professor and American Mathematics Association president Ravi Vakil posted a separate proof of the General Riemann Hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, which Vakil emphasized was "all human, with no AI." Masullo, who spent 12 years on the work, noted in an introduction that the project aimed to show that human mathematicians are still active amidst the current technological climate. Both announcements arrived during a notable week that also saw Anthropic become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab.
items.whyItMatters: This news highlights a major milestone at the intersection of advanced mathematics and AI, where a researcher used Anthropic's Claude to help solve a famous centuries-old problem, while a human-only parallel breakthrough underscored the ongoing role of traditional human scholarship.
items.whoIsAffected: Mathematicians, AI researchers, and developers working with automated reasoning tools and verification languages like Lean.

items.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
items.summary: On November 20, 2026, TechCrunch reported on the financial hurdles facing companies attempting to build data centers in space, specifically regarding chip financing and collateral. Traditional terrestrial data center ecosystems rely heavily on debt financing…
items.fullStory:
On November 20, 2026, TechCrunch reported on the financial hurdles facing companies attempting to build data centers in space, specifically regarding chip financing and collateral. Traditional terrestrial data center ecosystems rely heavily on debt financing where cloud providers borrow funds and use the physical chips as collateral, enabling lenders to repossess and resell the hardware if a default occurs. According to Compute Credit Index Research, older chips retain significant market value, with certain H100s selling for about half their original 2023 cost basis and H200 configurations maintaining their introduction prices.

However, lenders backing SpaceX's $40 billion chip financing deal reportedly requested that none of the purchased chips be used for orbital data center plans, as repossessing hardware located 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour is practically impossible. It remains unclear whether lenders successfully secured this provision from SpaceX. In the near term, SpaceX is focusing on deploying compute at terrestrial ground stations, with CEO Elon Musk dispatching rocket team engineers to accelerate infrastructure build-outs by addressing challenges like casting generator turbine blades faster than existing suppliers. Musk stated in early 2026 that he believes space will become the cheapest place to operate data centers within two to three years, though this depends heavily on achieving fully reusable configurations of the Starship rocket.

SpaceX faces ongoing technical and logistical challenges, including a recent flight test where the booster stage was not recovered, alongside terrestrial hurdles like finding land and power for ground-based data centers amid local opposition and project delays. Startups and companies like SpaceX, StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, and Orbital will need to purchase chips under potentially stricter financial terms than terrestrial counterparts, whereas Google is pursuing its own TPU chips in space via Project Suncatcher. Additionally, SpaceX and Tesla are collaborating on a U.S. chip foundry project named Terafab, which requires years of development and billions of dollars before reaching commercial semiconductor production at scale.
items.whyItMatters: The inability to use orbiting hardware as loan collateral introduces unique financial barriers and higher costs for space-based data center initiatives compared to terrestrial counterparts.
items.whoIsAffected: Space and AI infrastructure companies, equipment lenders, and hardware manufacturers.

items.fullStory:
On November 20, 2026, TechCrunch reporter Lauren Forristal published an overview of six AI-powered gadgets designed to upgrade the home office workspace. Tech companies are increasingly integrating artificial intelligence into everyday work tools, ranging from smart notetakers to automated webcams, to streamline productivity.

Among the highlighted products is the Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159), which combines traditional handwriting with audio recording, offering transcription, summarization, and a built-in 32GB storage capacity supporting 92 languages and up to 15 speakers. Another audio device is the Anker Soundcore Work ($159), a coin-sized recording pin providing up to eight hours of standalone battery life and companion app summaries, with optional Pro ($99/year) and Unlimited ($239/year) subscription plans. Logitech introduced its MX Keypad ($99) to bring dedicated AI shortcuts for tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex directly to users' desks. Meanwhile, Amazon launched the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($629), a color digital note-taking device featuring AI tools to clean up messy handwriting and summarize notes. For video calls, the Insta360 Link 2 Pro ($249) offers 4K video capture with intelligent tracking, automatic framing, and AI-powered noise cancellation. Finally, the Autonomous Desk Pro ($599) is an adjustable standing desk utilizing built-in sensors and AI to monitor user activity, track sitting versus standing habits, and monitor room CO2 levels.

The featured gadgets aim to assist professionals, researchers, students, and presenters by automating administrative tasks like note transcription, camera framing, and ergonomic tracking. The article notes that purchases made through links in the text may earn the publication a small commission.
items.whyItMatters: This news highlights the growing consumer hardware trend of embedding AI directly into everyday workspace accessories to automate administrative tasks and physical ergonomics. It showcases a diverse market of physical AI tools now available for remote workers and professionals.
items.whoIsAffected: Remote workers, professionals, students, and home office users looking to upgrade their productivity and workspace hardware.

items.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
items.summary: Apple is reportedly developing its own AI agent designed to perform computer tasks on behalf of users, such as using apps, accessing websites, and writing code. The project came to light on November 19, 2026, when Bloomberg spotted a job listing posted by App…
items.fullStory:
Apple is reportedly developing its own AI agent designed to perform computer tasks on behalf of users, such as using apps, accessing websites, and writing code. The project came to light on November 19, 2026, when Bloomberg spotted a job listing posted by Apple for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an "AI agent that can use a computer."

The job posting describes an agent that functions like a capable person by browsing the web, working across applications, running commands, writing and debugging code, and calling services privately. The posting states that the agent should move fluidly between tools and execute multi-step tasks across browsers, command lines, code, and APIs. TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment but received no response.

Computer-using agents have emerged as a major trend in the tech industry, with labs like Anthropic and OpenAI launching similar services, and Meta introducing its Muse agent line. Meanwhile, Bloomberg reports that Apple is simultaneously making it harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers by deploying warnings in macOS 27.3 to discourage users from granting full access. In October, Apple notified developers that it planned to introduce additional controls requiring explicit user action for apps seeking extraordinary access.

While Bloomberg notes that Apple has eyed introducing its in-house service as soon as the end of next year, progress on the project remains in the early stages.
items.whyItMatters: Apple's entry into the computer-using agent market highlights a major competitive push into autonomous AI workflows, while its stricter macOS controls for third-party agents raise questions about ecosystem openness.
items.whoIsAffected: Mac users, third-party AI developers, and Apple software engineering teams.

items.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
items.summary: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, November 19, 2026, raising a total of $81.3 billion, which included $1.95 billion for its seven founders. Each of the seven founders sold approximately 3.4 million shares at an upgraded IPO price of $83 per share…
items.fullStory:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, November 19, 2026, raising a total of $81.3 billion, which included $1.95 billion for its seven founders. Each of the seven founders sold approximately 3.4 million shares at an upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, netting about $280 million each before underwriting fees and taxes. This exceeded their initial target of around $250 million based on the midpoint price of $74 from the original price range. Anthropic noted in its filings that each founder has voluntarily pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity to philanthropy, though these commitments are revocable and not legally binding.

The public offering raised $104.8 billion for Anthropic's coffers, with a potential reach of $117 billion if bankers exercise all share allotments. This included the sale of $26 billion in special non-voting Class N stock to major tech industry players, with Nvidia and Google each purchasing $10 billion, while AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divided the remainder. Following the IPO, Google owns a 13.4% stake, and Amazon holds a 14.6% stake through converted promissory notes, bringing the combined stake of the two cloud providers to 28%.

Despite raising massive capital and gaining nearly $230 billion in available working capital, Anthropic disclosed extraordinary future financial requirements driven by infrastructure and compute demands. The company needs about $70.7 billion over the next 12 months as of September 30, 2026, and $451.6 billion before the end of 2030 to cover compute and infrastructure commitments. Overall, Anthropic has disclosed foreseeable infrastructure commitments totaling between $1.05 trillion and $1.08 trillion.
items.whyItMatters: Anthropic's record-breaking public debut underscores the staggering capital requirements and major tech-giant consolidation defining the generative AI landscape. The massive fundraise highlights both the immense financial scale of frontier AI operations and the unprecedented infrastructure costs required to sustain them.
items.whoIsAffected: Anthropic leadership, major cloud and hardware investors including Google, Amazon, and Nvidia, and public market investors.

items.title: Warehouse-level statement timeouts are now generally available

items.fullStory:
In November 2026, Databricks rolled out a series of feature releases and improvements across its platform, highlighted by the general availability of warehouse-level statement timeouts. Users can now set these timeouts using the statement_timeout field within the SQL warehouses API, Databricks SDKs, Terraform, or Declarative Automation Bundles. Additionally, account administrators can now configure retention periods ranging from 30 to 3,650 days for supported system tables, with the first 395 days provided for free before incurring storage charges.

Several machine learning and AI capabilities also received updates and new integrations. OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models became available on Unity Gateway, while OpenAI GPT-5 and GPT-5 mini were scheduled for retirement on December 11, 2026, with GPT-6.1 Sol recommended as a replacement. Google Gemini 3.6 Flash was retired on November 19, 2026, with automated redirection to Gemini 3.8 Flash. Furthermore, Genie Code CLI reached general availability, sharing a unified budget with workspace usage, and Genie ZeroOps entered beta to monitor jobs, pipelines, and tables in the background.

Governance, data sharing, and engineering pipelines saw notable expansions as well. Databricks-to-Databricks Delta Sharing expanded across regulatory domains to support commercial workspaces sharing with AWS GovCloud, AWS GovCloud DoD, and Azure China. In Lakeflow Connect, OAuth machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication became generally available for Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Jira connectors. Finally, pipeline flows became securable objects in Unity Catalog in beta, allowing granular permissions like READ FLOW and REFRESH FLOW to be managed on individual streams.
items.whyItMatters: These updates improve administrative control, governance across regulatory domains, and query management, while advancing Databricks' AI model offerings and developer workflows.
items.whoIsAffected: Databricks platform administrators, data engineers, data analysts, and AI/ML developers.

items.title: The Databricks GitHub app will request permission to create and manage pull requests

items.fullStory:
In an upcoming change, the Databricks GitHub app will request read and write access to pull requests to enable tools like Genie Code and Genie ZeroOps to create and manage pull requests on behalf of users. Databricks notes that existing branch protection rules and required reviews will still apply when these automated tools interact with repositories.

When this update occurs, owners of GitHub organizations and accounts with the app installed will receive a legitimate email from GitHub titled "Databricks is requesting updated permissions." Users who choose not to accept the new permissions will experience no change to their current workflows, retaining the ability to clone, pull, commit, and push code manually.

Without accepting the updated permissions, the only functional limitation is that Genie Code and Genie ZeroOps will be unable to automatically create and manage pull requests for the user. Affected users can consult the official documentation on connecting a Git provider to Databricks for further guidance.
items.whyItMatters: This update enables AI coding and automation tools like Genie Code and Genie ZeroOps to seamlessly manage pull requests, streamlining developer workflows on the platform.
items.whoIsAffected: GitHub organization owners, account owners, and developers using Genie Code or Genie ZeroOps.

items.title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
items.summary: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini, a new looped transformer model designed for local AI setups. The model is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts featuring approximately 26 billion physical total parameters and 3 billion active parameters per token…
items.fullStory:
Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini, a new looped transformer model designed for local AI setups. The model is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts featuring approximately 26 billion physical total parameters and 3 billion active parameters per token. It uses a unique looping architecture where the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop, allowing the model to act as if it has 48 logical layers while utilizing only 24 physical decoder layers. It supports a 1-million-token context size, accepts both image and text inputs, and includes a DSpark drafter for additional speed-up.

Alongside the flagship model, a research artifact variant named TML-d24-varloop-research was also released, which is trained to accept a variable number of loops for faster inference at a potential cost to quality. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights, and Day-zero inference support is provided by SGLang for production deployments on datacenter hardware, alongside support for transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX.

In benchmark evaluations, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 out of 48 categories against models such as Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL within the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. It shows strong performance in coding tasks, agentic search, and vision interpretation. Developers can access GGUF 4-bit and 8-bit quantizations and integrate the model using frameworks like Hugging Face transformers and Llama App.
items.whyItMatters: Inkling 2 Mini introduces an innovative looped Mixture-of-Experts architecture that delivers state-of-the-art local performance and a 1M-token context window in a compact, efficient footprint.
items.whoIsAffected: AI developers, researchers, and local AI users looking to run efficient multimodal models.

items.title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
items.summary: On November 20, 2026, Hugging Face researchers published a technique called "harness adapters," which applies reinforcement learning (RL) directly inside standard agent harnesses to optimize base models for specific workloads, improving both performance and c…
items.fullStory:
On November 20, 2026, Hugging Face researchers published a technique called "harness adapters," which applies reinforcement learning (RL) directly inside standard agent harnesses to optimize base models for specific workloads, improving both performance and cost. The authors, including Younes Belkada, Lewis Tunstall, and others, demonstrated that while models target general performance, combining a model with a specific harness leaves efficiency on the table. By freezing base weights and adding a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter, models can reason less, call fewer tools, and achieve higher pass rates.

To showcase the approach, the team targeted the Qwen3.8-27B model across three distinct agent harnesses: Pi, OpenCode, and Hermes Agent. For the Qwen3.8-27B model running on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the Pi harness, the base score of 39% (using 2.9K tokens per task) increased to a 55% pass@1 score while dropping average token usage to 1.5K. The workflow utilized TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv, and Harbor on Hugging Face Jobs to generate, validate, and train on custom agentic coding task distributions.

The task creation pipeline drew from three sources: SWE-smith (injecting bugs into real Python and Go repositories), SWE-Gym (converting GitHub issues and merged fixes into tasks via TaskTrove), and Tasksmith (generating tasks from merged pull requests). Out of 1,127 Hub candidates, 858 passed initial metadata and semantic validation using `openenv validate`. A subsequent difficulty check using Qwen3.8-27B further filtered the tasks to those solved only sometimes (171 tasks out of 442 scored), ensuring effective learning signals for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Finally, the team merged the three individual harness LoRAs into a single "super adapter" that runs unchanged under Pi, Hermes Agent, and OpenCode. All resulting artifacts, including adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, and the safeagents plugin, have been released in a public Hugging Face collection for community re-use.
items.whyItMatters: Harness adapters prove that training models with RL directly inside native agent frameworks significantly boosts task performance while drastically cutting token consumption and inference costs. This reusable recipe empowers developers to squeeze maximum efficiency out of any open model for their specific toolchains.
items.whoIsAffected: AI engineers, MLOps practitioners, and developers building autonomous agents using open-source models and standard evaluation harnesses.

items.title: Why PostgreSQL 19 shipped late
items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 shipped approximately a month after its usual September to October window for major releases, with the delay driven by the project's focus on quality amid a surge in AI-discovered bugs. Written by Jonathan Katz and Robert Haas and published on N…
items.fullStory:
PostgreSQL 19 shipped approximately a month after its usual September to October window for major releases, with the delay driven by the project's focus on quality amid a surge in AI-discovered bugs. Written by Jonathan Katz and Robert Haas and published on November 19, 2026, the article explains that starting around February 2026, AI tools made finding bugs and security issues significantly easier. Consequently, CVEs fixed per quarterly update release surged from a historical range of one to four up to 28 by August 2026, while commits back-patched to the release branch increased by 61% and back-patches to prior release branches jumped by 74%. Contributors had to spend critical time fixing these discovered bugs rather than reviewing new features, resulting in the release timeline slipping as features not ready in time were deferred.

Despite the delay, PostgreSQL 19 is now generally available and introduces several key features: REPACK for rebuilding bloated tables during normal read and write operations, query plan advice for stabilizing critical query plans without altering application SQL, WAIT FOR LSN for read-your-writes functionality on replicas without polling or arbitrary sleeps, and logical replication support for synchronizing sequences to eliminate migration friction. The November 12 update release for supported branches ultimately included so many fixes that the release team issued a second release candidate to ensure PostgreSQL 19 shipped with them.

The authors note that the PostgreSQL project is actively adapting to this new landscape where LLMs scrutinize software. While AI has made finding bugs much easier, fixing them remains a human task that strains contributor bandwidth. Looking ahead, the community views this heightened AI scrutiny as a permanent shift in open-source development and an unprecedented opportunity to make PostgreSQL more reliable than ever before.
items.whyItMatters: The late release of PostgreSQL 19 illustrates a broader industry shift where the widespread use of LLMs for vulnerability discovery drastically increases bug-fix volume and strains maintainer bandwidth in open-source software.
items.whoIsAffected: PostgreSQL developers, open-source maintainers, and database administrators managing PostgreSQL deployments.

items.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
items.summary: Meta plans to charge $300 for its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device called Muse Charm, according to a report published by The Information on November 19, 2026. The device was initially teased at Meta's Connect event earlier this year. When reached for commen…
items.fullStory:
Meta plans to charge $300 for its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device called Muse Charm, according to a report published by The Information on November 19, 2026. The device was initially teased at Meta's Connect event earlier this year. When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson did not deny the claims, stating, "We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon."

Meta has previously launched Muse, an agentic helper accompanied by cute avatars that give the system a personality. Muse Charm represents Meta's expansion into AI hardware, designed to let users carry a physical personification of the software in their pocket or wear it around their neck. The device allows users to talk to it, ask questions, and give commands.

The $300 price point for the keychain-sized product is comparable to other offerings in the market, such as the AI wearable by startup Friend which retails for $250. However, it is significantly higher than Amazon's Bee Frontier wearable AI device, which lists for $75 and features a Black Friday sale price of $52.49, alongside a $99 per year subscription.
items.whyItMatters: This report reveals Meta's hardware pricing strategy for its upcoming consumer AI wearable, positioning it against competing devices in a challenging market sector.
items.whoIsAffected: Consumer hardware buyers and technology enthusiasts interested in AI wearables.

items.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
items.summary: Over the past two weeks, top U.S. businesses and critical infrastructure faced a wave of technical outages disrupting everyday life. Incidents included Apple Pay going down, NASA's internal communication network failing, the FAA grounding all flights for hour…
items.fullStory:
Over the past two weeks, top U.S. businesses and critical infrastructure faced a wave of technical outages disrupting everyday life. Incidents included Apple Pay going down, NASA's internal communication network failing, the FAA grounding all flights for hours in only the third such occurrence since 9/11, and Microsoft suffering an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days. While the Director of National Intelligence stated the outages did not appear related to state-sponsored terrorism and President Trump called them individual events, the close timing followed Cybersecurity's 'Black October' on October 21, which struck PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, and others.

Dave DeWalt, an investor and former cybersecurity CEO, noted that the technical disruptions are likely growing pains from a security system getting stronger rather than weaker, as AI surfaces vulnerabilities at an unprecedented speed through tools like Mythos and others. Enterprises are rushing to fix long-standing technical flaws before bad actors can exploit them, and that surge in patching is causing short-term disruptions. Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of Corsha, stated that industrial systems were never designed to be securely connected in the modern way, pointing out that the FAA outage may have stemmed from trying to modernize telecommunications infrastructure where new tech operated at normal capacity while legacy hardware could not keep up.

Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, wrote on X that the disruptions should serve as a wake-up call, stating that AI is moving faster than society's ability to manage its consequences. Iyer emphasized that the issue is not rapid AI adoption itself, but rather the rushed mix of legacy and modern systems without clear risk understanding. Experts recommend a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including better testing, prioritized fixes, and tighter segmentation and access control for industrial systems.

DeWalt pointed to a silver lining, noting he prefers enterprises finding and patching flaws messily over bad actors exploiting them for national security threats. He also expects a rise in startups focused on AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing, and critical infrastructure resilience.
items.whyItMatters: A wave of major outages across U.S. infrastructure and enterprises highlights the dangerous friction of rushing to merge modern AI and patching workflows with aging legacy systems.
items.whoIsAffected: Enterprise IT teams, critical infrastructure operators, and cybersecurity professionals.

items.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
items.summary: In November 2026, Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a series of unfolding personal and national security controversies. U.S. officials stated that one of Huang's romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who…
items.fullStory:
In November 2026, Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a series of unfolding personal and national security controversies. U.S. officials stated that one of Huang's romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who fed information to Beijing. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips, and its ties to China became the subject of investigations by the U.S. Justice Department and Congress.

The scandal escalated when reports surfaced that Huang had additional extramarital affairs, including relationships with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell and an unnamed third Nvidia employee. Amid the fallout, Nvidia's board prepared to oust Huang, leading to his resignation on November 12, 2026. CFO Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones was named the company's first-ever chair of the board of directors. Following his ouster, Huang agreed to testify before Congress regarding the national security implications of his relationships and export controls.

Despite the leadership shakeup, Nvidia reported strong third-quarter earnings of $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Interim CEO Colette Kress stated that the company plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year and announced that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending its participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban. Meanwhile, Huang publicly stated on November 17, 2026, that he would be honored to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, and America, though board chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that reinstating Huang is not currently under consideration.
items.whyItMatters: The sudden departure of Nvidia's CEO amid national security investigations and geopolitical tensions surrounding chip exports to China marks a critical leadership crisis for the world's leading AI hardware maker.
items.whoIsAffected: Nvidia executives, employees, board members, investors, and U.S. and international policymakers.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156B to charity
items.summary: On November 19, 2026, journalist Tim Fernholz reported on Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), which could direct up to $156 billion to charitable causes through a combination of the company's Public Benefit Fund (PBF) and employee pledge ma…
items.fullStory:
On November 19, 2026, journalist Tim Fernholz reported on Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), which could direct up to $156 billion to charitable causes through a combination of the company's Public Benefit Fund (PBF) and employee pledge matching. Anthropic's leadership, rooted in effective altruism, structured the market debut to fund philanthropic efforts focused on AI safety, worker impact, and other initiatives. At an IPO price of $83 and a current trading price of about $95, the PBF's allotted 5% stake—nearly 850 million shares—gives it an endowment valued at $80 billion. Furthermore, the PBF can receive additional 2% share increases whenever the valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price. The PBF's initial commitments include $200 million to study AI's impact on workers, alongside potential future funding for philanthropic organizations, direct distributions, or universal basic income plans. Additionally, Anthropic donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco, though a company spokesperson clarified that this separate donation did not originate from the PBF.

In addition to the PBF, Anthropic employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes, with the company committing to match those donations 3-to-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. According to the company's S-1 filing, more than 550 million shares were reserved to fulfill pledges made before September 30. Based on disclosures that 84% of these shares were reserved for early employee matches, employee pledges are estimated at $23 billion, accompanied by roughly $53 billion in company matching funds depending on the stock price at delivery. For context, these combined funds total $156 billion, which equals approximately a quarter of the $617 billion donated to charity by Americans in 2025.

Realizing this total depends on employees fulfilling their pledges and the timing of Anthropic's matching donations, with some shares potentially flowing into donor-advised funds that could limit immediate impact. Interviews indicate that donors are expected to support effective altruism-aligned charities such as Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can, with significant allocations directed toward AI safety research.
items.whyItMatters: Anthropic's IPO structure establishes a historic precedent for corporate philanthropy by tying a major frontier AI lab's market debut to massive funding for effective altruism, AI safety, and worker impact research.
items.whoIsAffected: Anthropic employees, effective altruism charities, and philanthropic organizations focused on AI safety and worker impacts.

items.title: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
items.summary: Google announced on Thursday that it is bringing computer use capabilities to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing the AI to complete tasks on behalf of users by navigating native Mac applications and browsing websites in the background. The feat…
items.fullStory:
Google announced on Thursday that it is bringing computer use capabilities to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing the AI to complete tasks on behalf of users by navigating native Mac applications and browsing websites in the background. The feature enables the AI to handle multistep workflows involving local files, apps, and the web after receiving instructions from the user. Users can watch the agent work via a live preview in their chat while keeping their own screen and cursor free, with controls available to pause, stop, or approve actions before they occur.

Google suggests the new computer use feature is useful for tedious workflows such as filling out forms, repeating tasks across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, and creating slideshows from files or online dashboards. This launch follows Google's broader rollout of Gemini's in-app "Tasks" feature for signing into websites, making purchases, and booking appointments, alongside early testing of its revamped "CC" AI agent announced in September.

The feature is initially available in English for users in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac along with a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. Google did not disclose when the capability will expand to other markets or platforms, and enters a competitive space where other leading model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta already offer agentic desktop features.
items.whyItMatters: Bringing computer use capabilities to the Gemini Mac app helps Google catch up to competitors offering agentic desktop features, expanding AI assistance into local file management and native application workflows.
items.whoIsAffected: U.S.-based macOS users with Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscriptions using the Gemini desktop app.

items.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
items.summary: Meta employees have raised concerns that the company's AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a Reuters report published on November 19, 2026, which reviewed internal company posts…
items.fullStory:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company's AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a Reuters report published on November 19, 2026, which reviewed internal company posts. Internal reports detailed instances where Muse surfaced messages regarding unrequested childcare requests, unasked career advice, unplaced product orders, and incorrect bank account balances. One employee noted that Muse randomly sent an extra message in a weather and tide chat displaying specific Capital One and Charles Schwab bank balances, while another employee reported receiving an unprompted reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, describing it as an extreme privacy violation without granted app access.

A Meta spokesperson stated in an email to TechCrunch that employee testing is fundamental to product development to gather feedback for safety and privacy protections, noting that employees access different versions of Muse with features and functionality not available to the general public. Launched in September, Muse has achieved over 10 million downloads, making it one of the fastest-growing apps on record.

The reported data mixing issues during internal testing highlight ongoing privacy challenges in deploying consumer-facing generative AI agents at scale. Meta's response emphasizes that internal testing protocols are designed to catch and address such behaviors before wider public exposure.
items.whyItMatters: This news matters because it exposes critical privacy vulnerabilities and cross-account data leaks in one of the fastest-growing consumer AI agents on the market.
items.whoIsAffected: Meta employees, app users, and individuals whose private data or messages may be inadvertently exposed.

items.fullStory:
Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup connecting smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories, announced on November 19, 2026, that it has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding. The funding round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed. Co-founded in 2024 by former Alibaba executive Sisi Song and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, the company is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year. Everful currently ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries, works with over 30,000 factory partners, and maintains an online wholesale catalog featuring more than 20 million products.

The startup differentiates itself from traditional marketplaces and platforms like Alibaba and Faire by managing the entire sourcing process end-to-end. As co-founder Kevin Han stated, “We take care of everything. We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That's something the marketplaces don't offer.” Everful utilizes AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics. The platform is designed for smaller retailers and brands that lack dedicated sourcing teams.

Operating across borders, Everful must navigate trade tensions and shifting policies, such as the Trump administration's suspension of the de minimis exemption that previously allowed shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the U.S. duty-free. Sisi Song noted that the company factored geopolitical issues into its strategy from day one, aiming to combine overseas sourcing with local retail sales. Everful employs about 70 full-time staff globally, including 45 in research and development, and has established an AI operations team to connect engineering and business functions.

With the new Series A capital, Everful plans to expand its presence in the U.S. and Europe—specifically the U.K., France, and Italy—while investing further in AI to automate product customization and sourcing workflows. The company also aims to deepen integrations with e-commerce platforms, building upon its existing Shopify integration as it works toward becoming an end-to-end infrastructure platform for global sourcing.
items.whyItMatters: This significant funding round highlights how AI agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex global supply chain and cross-border manufacturing workflows for smaller businesses. It also demonstrates how startups are attempting to outmaneuver macroeconomic trade hurdles through tech-enabled operational integration.
items.whoIsAffected: Smaller retailers, brands without dedicated sourcing teams, and cross-border e-commerce operators.

On November 19, 2026, shares of Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq exchange following a successful initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares traded at $111.50, representing a 33% premium over the initial public offering price of $83. The offering price, set on Wednesday, exceeded the company's projected range of $70 to $78 per share.

The public offering raises over $81 billion, which will be directed to employees and the company's coffers. Combined with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed alongside the public market debut, Anthropic is left with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. An analyst noted to TechCrunch that the company will have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.

While share prices continue to fluctuate, the opening price places Anthropic's market capitalization at over $2 trillion, surpassing Meta, Tesla, and Walmart, leaving only Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft with higher valuations.

In a speech before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company's commitment to safety, stating that the stronger financial position strengthens their resolve to make the right choices on safety while building a successful company, which he termed a "race to the top."
items.whyItMatters: Anthropic's massive public market debut and historic cash reserves position it as one of the most valuable corporations globally, testing the scale of AI financing and enterprise valuation.

items.fullStory:
On Thursday, Anthropic made its Wall Street debut in the largest IPO in history. Speaking at the Nasdaq opening bell ceremony, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company's commitment to responsible AI development, vowing that the firm would not bend to business or political pressure and would remain under human control.

Reading from a prepared speech, Amodei reflected on Anthropic's origins, mentioning how he and co-founder Daniela Amodei were inspired to build beneficial technology after losing their father to a disease that later became curable. He highlighted AI's potential to accelerate medical and scientific progress—suggesting it could compress a century of progress into a decade—while also addressing the technology's serious risks, including misuse by bad actors, economic disruption, and losing control of systems.

Amodei explicitly committed to pacing the training and deployment of Anthropic's AI systems, taking as long as necessary to ensure safety. He stressed that the most difficult safety work lies ahead, requiring talent to be directed toward double- and triple-checking model safety. Co-founder Daniela Amodei echoed these sentiments in a CNBC interview, emphasizing the company's ongoing dedication to mitigating risks despite the incredible promise of AI.
items.whyItMatters: As Anthropic goes public in a historic IPO, its leadership is publicly doubling down on safety-first development and pacing model releases despite market pressures. This public stance sets a high-profile benchmark for corporate responsibility and governance in the rapidly scaling AI industry.
items.whoIsAffected: Anthropic leadership, employees, investors, and customers relying on Claude, alongside competitors watching industry safety standards.

items.title: Bulk migrate your dashboards to AI/BI with Genie Code
items.summary: On November 19, 2026, Databricks engineering authors Dipankar Kushari and Archana Shetty announced the general availability of bulk migration capabilities for dashboards using Genie Code. This feature allows organizations to move an entire folder of Tableau o…
items.fullStory:
On November 19, 2026, Databricks engineering authors Dipankar Kushari and Archana Shetty announced the general availability of bulk migration capabilities for dashboards using Genie Code. This feature allows organizations to move an entire folder of Tableau or Power BI reports to Databricks AI/BI Dashboards in a single run using the /importBI command, eliminating the manual process of migrating reports individually.

To perform a bulk migration, users export their BI reports—supporting formats such as .twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx, .pbit, or .tmdl—and stage the files within a directory inside a Unity Catalog volume. From a draft dashboard, users open Genie Code and run the /importBI command directed at that volume directory or issue a natural language request. The migration agent matches workbooks with data source files, prompts for the target catalog and schema, and processes reports in queued batches while reusing existing Unity Catalog tables, views, and metric views.

A status card tracks the batch progress, marking each report as Queued, Running, or Completed, and permits halting individual reports or the entire batch. Once generated, users can review individual reports through dedicated Genie Code tabs, follow the migration plan, refine dashboards using follow-up prompts, and validate results against original dashboards using screenshots or a read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) connection. The authors recommend best practices such as connecting source BI tools via MCP, staging data-source definitions alongside workbooks, ensuring underlying data is reachable in Databricks, and promoting local metric views to Unity Catalog for reuse.
items.whyItMatters: Bulk migration removes the manual bottleneck of converting reports individually, allowing organizations to scale dashboard modernization efforts from a months-long grind to a repeatable, folder-at-a-time workflow.
items.whoIsAffected: Data analysts, BI teams, and administrators migrating legacy Tableau and Power BI reports to Databricks AI/BI.

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase
items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 is now available on Lakebase on the exact day of its community release, allowing customers to access the new version immediately rather than waiting weeks as is common with other managed PostgreSQL services. Several Lakebase engineers, who are o…
items.fullStory:
PostgreSQL 19 is now available on Lakebase on the exact day of its community release, allowing customers to access the new version immediately rather than waiting weeks as is common with other managed PostgreSQL services. Several Lakebase engineers, who are official PostgreSQL committers and contributors, worked directly on this release, contributing to query plan advice, shared memory, locale handling, and release management. To try the new version, users can create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19.

This release focuses primarily on operational control, targeting persistent database challenges such as bloated tables, unstable query plans, replica lag, incomplete statistics, and difficult production maintenance. Key features include REPACK, which reclaims space and physically orders rows while normal reads and writes continue, replacing the need for external tools or downtime-heavy locking commands. Additionally, PostgreSQL 19 introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice to help database teams stabilize inaccurate query execution plans by applying advice outside of application query text.

Further enhancements in PostgreSQL 19 include parallel autovacuum capabilities, new performance statistics views like pg_stat_lock and pg_stat_recovery, logical replication upgrades such as sequence synchronization, and the WAIT FOR LSN function which enables read-your-writes behavior on read replicas. Other updates cover statistics import for postgres_fdw, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for efficient get-or-create patterns, and direct JSON output for COPY TO. To use the new features, users must create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19.
items.whyItMatters: Making PostgreSQL 19 available on Lakebase on day one gives database teams immediate access to critical operational controls like REPACK and query plan advice without the typical multi-week wait of other managed services.
items.whoIsAffected: Lakebase database teams, engineers, and developers managing PostgreSQL workloads on Databricks.

items.fullStory:
Databricks has released several updates for Lakebase, its fully managed Postgres database service, spanning from August 5 through November 19, 2026. On November 19, Lakebase added support for Postgres 19, which can be selected when creating a new project. This follows a November 12 update that rolled out minor Postgres versions 18.7, 17.12, and 16.16 less than 30 minutes after the PostgreSQL community released them. Earlier, on October 26, the Lakebase snapshots API and backup schedule API became generally available, allowing users to programmatically manage point-in-time snapshots and automated backup cadences.

Additional updates include the beta transition of Lakebase Insights to per-project settings on October 19, providing telemetry-based diagnostics and recommendations using system.lakebase tables. On October 15, Lakebase Search added support for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) full-text search via the lakebase_tokenizer extension (version 0.2.0) and introduced native Postgres logical replication to stream changes in and out of Lakebase. Furthermore, Lakebase Search achieved general availability on September 18, bringing scalable vector search (lakebase_vector) and BM25 full-text search (lakebase_text) to projects. Compliance enhancements were also rolled out, making Lakebase PCI-DSS and HITRUST compliant in all AWS regions for workspaces with the compliance security profile enabled, alongside the default enablement of Lakebase in compliance workspaces starting August 5.

Performance and usability features were introduced throughout the period, including LTAP Direct Writes in beta on August 25 to accelerate synced table loads by writing directly to the storage layer. On August 24, Genie Code became available in the Lakebase project UI via the sidebar, enabling users to perform multi-step data and AI tasks using natural language. Additionally, programmatic management through the REST API, Databricks CLI, and SDKs became generally available on August 14, and supported Postgres extensions—such as PostGIS and hll—received version updates on September 30.
items.whyItMatters: These updates significantly expand Lakebase's enterprise capabilities, developer tooling, and global compliance standards, making the fully managed Postgres service more powerful and versatile for building applications on Databricks.

items.title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
items.summary: On November 18, 2026, RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B, its first model built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using the Miles framework. Authored by Jason Chen, the announcement details that the model was trained on long-horizon agent ta…
items.fullStory:
On November 18, 2026, RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B, its first model built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using the Miles framework. Authored by Jason Chen, the announcement details that the model was trained on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1 million tokens, utilizing just 1,200 curated tasks over 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B is available under the Apache 2.0 license in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 formats, retaining the original Qwen architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window while incorporating default thinking behavior in its outputs.

The model demonstrates performance gains across multiple reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks compared to the base Qwen3.8-27B. Notably, DaisyRose-27B improves the Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 score from 5.6% to 12.0%, and achieves increases on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (75.5% versus 73.0%), DeepSWE v1.1 (46.2% versus 42.2%), SWE Bench Pro v2 (94.7% versus 91.3%), HLE text-only (34.3% versus 33.9%), IFBench (82.4% versus 79.5%), and GPQA Diamond (90.7% versus 89.2%). RadixArk recommends serving the model using SGLang with DSpark speculative decoding.

Three foundational pillars enabled the release: high-quality training data built in partnership with Eigent AI from thousands of candidates narrowed down to 1,200 targeted tasks; an efficient asynchronous training backend called Miles that achieved 37% model FLOPs utilization and 57% lower training costs; and a robust sandbox service built on AgentENV that ran approximately 944,000 sandboxes with a 99.95% success rate since late October. RadixArk credits the Eigent AI team for task collaboration, the Qwen team for the base model, and contributions from various open-source communities.
items.whyItMatters: The release demonstrates a highly efficient reinforcement learning post-training pipeline for long-horizon AI agents that significantly cuts GPU time and costs while improving performance across key benchmarks.
items.whoIsAffected: AI developers, researchers, and engineers building and deploying large language models and agentic workflows.

items.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
items.summary: On November 18, 2026, Hugging Face's Dharma-AI team published an article analyzing why end-to-end fine-tuning times for generative language models often exceed standard FLOP-based estimates. The authors noted that traditional methods rely on compute-only form…
items.fullStory:
On November 18, 2026, Hugging Face's Dharma-AI team published an article analyzing why end-to-end fine-tuning times for generative language models often exceed standard FLOP-based estimates. The authors noted that traditional methods rely on compute-only formulas that fail to account for real-world overheads such as environment setup, model downloads, tokenization, periodic evaluations, checkpoint uploads, and network and storage I/O contention on shared clusters. To investigate this discrepancy, the team evaluated 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from a production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, totaling approximately 7,382 GPU-hours, with durations ranging from 1.6 to 172.4 hours.

The research compared traditional analytical approaches against learned machine learning predictors using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The standard FLOP baseline yielded poor results (R² = 0.31, MAE = 12.41 hours at 30% MFU), and an extended version of the Calculon analytical performance model accounted for a median of only 11% of observed wall-clock time. In contrast, a CatBoost regressor trained exclusively on pre-dispatch configuration features achieved an R² of 0.98, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.71 hours, and a median error of 0.51 hours. Feature importance analysis revealed that variables outside the core optimization loop—such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, and dataset size—heavily influence actual execution time.

While the current CatBoost model is specifically calibrated to NVIDIA H200 infrastructure and is limited to SFT jobs up to 15 billion parameters, the methodology transfers overhead-aware feature design to cluster scheduling. The team plans to release a full academic paper on arXiv soon, with future steps including the incorporation of hardware-specific descriptors, validation on other GPU types, and expansion to additional training objectives such as RLHF and DPO.
items.whyItMatters: Accurately predicting fine-tuning duration eliminates scheduling guesswork on expensive GPU clusters, reducing costly idle time and preventing downstream delivery delays. By proving that pre-dispatch machine learning models drastically outperform traditional FLOP calculations, this research offers a practical blueprint for optimizing multi-tenant AI infrastructure.
items.whoIsAffected: ML engineers, MLOps teams, and cluster administrators managing shared GPU infrastructure.

items.summary: IBM Research and Confluent announced on November 18, 2026, the native integration of IBM time-series foundation models—which boast more than 50 million downloads—into Confluent's data streaming platform. The integration enables organizations to run predictive…
items.fullStory:
IBM Research and Confluent announced on November 18, 2026, the native integration of IBM time-series foundation models—which boast more than 50 million downloads—into Confluent's data streaming platform. The integration enables organizations to run predictive forecasting, anomaly detection, and semantic intelligence directly on streaming data using Apache Flink and SQL, operating natively on standard CPUs both in the cloud and on premises without requiring specialized GPUs.

The collaboration addresses the challenge of turning continuous business observations into real-time decisions. By embedding pre-trained foundation models directly into the Streamhouse architecture, enterprises can scale model development without training separate models for every individual series, refresh predictions continuously as data streams in, and route signals closer to operational decisions. The article highlights six mission-critical use cases across industries: optimizing ice cream production lines by forecasting product specs, detecting retail sales anomalies, improving supply chain planning across every SKU and store, adding personalized spending behavior to card payment fraud workflows, pacing trading execution against real-time volume forecasts, and performing semantic similarity searches on sensor patterns.

Looking ahead, IBM and Confluent position this architecture for the agentic era, where AI agents, applications, analytics, and lakehouses can leverage low-latency context from Lightning Tables and Flink pipelines. The deployment aims to simplify infrastructure by running compact models alongside streaming pipelines, reducing the need for dedicated GPU hardware while maintaining audit trails and business guardrails.
items.whyItMatters: Integrating pre-trained time-series foundation models natively into streaming platforms allows enterprises to execute real-time forecasting and anomaly detection on standard CPUs without deploying GPUs or training custom models for every data stream.
items.whoIsAffected: Enterprise data engineers, process engineers, supply chain planners, application developers, and AI agents operating within manufacturing, retail, banking, and trading sectors.

items.title: How we raised Databricks cluster rate limits by 7.5×
items.summary: The Compute Platform team at Databricks transitioned from fixed request-rate limits to adaptive concurrency limits for cluster creation in classic compute, raising default request-rate limits by 7.5× and removing over a hundred customer-specific overrides. Hi…
items.fullStory:
The Compute Platform team at Databricks transitioned from fixed request-rate limits to adaptive concurrency limits for cluster creation in classic compute, raising default request-rate limits by 7.5× and removing over a hundred customer-specific overrides. Historically, the platform protected services with fixed rate-rate limits tested against different load patterns. However, these static limits often turned away customer requests when capacity was available or continued accepting requests when cloud dependencies slowed down, forcing engineers to manually adjust limits during incidents.

To solve this, the team implemented adaptive concurrency limits that track unfinished work and changing system health rather than just counting API requests. In this new model, asynchronous cluster-creation workflows must acquire a slot to run, and the system dynamically adjusts the number of available slots based on operational signals such as provisioning duration and thread pool saturation. When dependencies degrade, the controller reduces concurrent workflows to prevent retry storms, while a bounded queue absorbs short bursts. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains in place only as a final safety guardrail against extreme incoming traffic.

By distinguishing between system degradation and excessive tenant demand, the platform provides clearer metrics for operators and customers. The new approach allows customers to run at full throttle when cloud capacity permits while easing off during degradation to maintain steady progress. This transition ultimately enabled Databricks to increase default cluster-creation request-rate limits by 7.5× and eliminate the maintenance overhead of managing numerous custom overrides.
items.whyItMatters: Moving from fixed rate limits to adaptive concurrency limits allows Databricks to safely increase default cluster-creation capacity by 7.5× while preventing retry storms during cloud provider outages.
items.whoIsAffected: Databricks customers launching clusters and the Compute Platform team maintaining infrastructure.

items.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
items.summary: On November 18, 2026, Hugging Face developer Tarek Ziadé detailed an experiment pushing Mixture of Experts (MoE) model inference to the limit using Transformers on a 32GB MacBook M5. Ziadé tackled the challenge of running massive models—specifically the 180-p…
items.fullStory:
On November 18, 2026, Hugging Face developer Tarek Ziadé detailed an experiment pushing Mixture of Experts (MoE) model inference to the limit using Transformers on a 32GB MacBook M5. Ziadé tackled the challenge of running massive models—specifically the 180-parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model containing 121GB of experts—on consumer hardware with limited unified memory. By default, standard engines like llama.cpp, vLLM, and Transformers struggle with massive MoE offloading due to lack of caching, inefficient routing, or severe PCIe bottlenecks.

To bridge this gap, Ziadé developed a custom expert-streaming approach integrated into Hugging Face's Transformers via pull request #50717. The solution uses an LRU cache turned into a slot pool, allowing grouped matrix multiplication (grouped_mm) to run natively without custom expert kernels. Additionally, experts were quantized offline to 3 bits (reducing them to 49GB on disk with a 12 GiB device cache), dense layers were quantized to 8 bits, and the system utilized 8 I/O threads to prefetch experts by reading routers early.

After optimizations including Metal kernels, PyTorch MPS commit forcing, and adopting Strata's GGUF weights, the custom Transformers setup achieved impressive benchmark results on the 32GB Mac. It reached 13.9 tok/s on short decode (compared to Strata's 14.8 tok/s), 228 tok/s on a 4K prefill prompt, and 12.4 tok/s on decode after a 6K document. Ziadé noted that the remaining performance gap is largely due to host round trips and limitations in PyTorch's MPS stream regarding GPU and CPU synchronization.

Ziadé released the code in a Hugging Face Space called tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming and submitted the core changes to the official Transformers repository. Next steps involve discussing the API with Transformers maintainers, potentially merging quantized expert features into per-layer quantization plans, and addressing PyTorch MPS limitations.
items.whyItMatters: This breakthrough demonstrates that massive 180B parameter MoE models can run efficiently on consumer hardware like a 32GB Mac using standard tools like Transformers, significantly lowering the barrier for local AI development.
items.whoIsAffected: AI developers, researchers, and local hardware enthusiasts running large Mixture of Experts models on consumer devices.

items.title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
items.summary: On November 18, 2026, researchers Reson8 (including contributors Reson8, Mark 't Hart, Eustache Le Bihan, and Eric Bezzam) open-sourced Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It is a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model designed for over 40 languages…
items.fullStory:
On November 18, 2026, researchers Reson8 (including contributors Reson8, Mark 't Hart, Eustache Le Bihan, and Eric Bezzam) open-sourced Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It is a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model designed for over 40 languages. The model features native support in 🤗 Transformers and vLLM without custom code, automatic language detection, and output control such as numbers as digits or words, fillers, verbatim repeats, and forced language.

Built using the Qwen3-ASR architecture, Rumble-2-Flash was created by distilling a larger production model, Rumble-2, using on-policy distillation combined with a technique called GOLD to bridge tokenizer differences between the teacher and student models. The creators tested how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off by having the student transcribe audio itself while the teacher graded transcripts token by token.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash achieved an average error rate of 6.96% across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch, and English, outperforming Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B and Whisper large-v3. It achieved 6.6% WER on the English track and processing speeds reaching over 7,000 RTFx on full batches, transcribing an hour of audio in about half a second. On AppTek's 302-hour call-centre benchmark featuring 14 English accents, it reached 7.86% WER, performing on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B).

The model weights are available on the Hugging Face Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash, and the model is also accessible through an API. The creators invited community feedback and project sharing in the Discussions tab.
items.whyItMatters: Rumble-2-Flash demonstrates that a tiny 0.5B-parameter speech model can match the performance of models up to 60 times its size while running exceptionally fast and efficiently on standard infrastructure.
items.whoIsAffected: Software developers, AI engineers, and enterprises building speech recognition and audio transcription applications.

items.fullStory:
On November 17, 2026, Databricks published a field guide highlighting eleven customer projects from its latest Lakebase hackathon. The event focused on Databricks Lakebase, a fully managed Postgres database built for the lakehouse with separated storage and compute, operating under Unity Catalog governance.

The hackathon was split into two main tracks: Track 1 centered on application development and database branching, while Track 2 concentrated on syncing data and real-time serving. Participants included teams from Lyft, CIBC, Arbital Health, OneTrust, Reach Mobile, Markel, Data Axle, and Sobeys. Notable projects included Lyft's 'Jevons Search'—which used copy-on-write branching to give AI agents a safe production copy for processing support tickets in about six seconds—and Data Axle's 'PriceWise', which utilized synced tables and pgvector embeddings to deliver vacation rental pricing suggestions in as little as 4 milliseconds.

Stated consequences and outcomes from the hackathon demonstrated how Lakebase eliminates the need for separate systems like auxiliary search indices or slow staging databases. Projects successfully replaced traditional setups by combining operational database capabilities with lakehouse governance, allowing teams to test schema changes, spin up preview environments in under five seconds, and unify analytics with real-time application serving.
items.whyItMatters: The Lakebase hackathon demonstrates how operational Postgres databases can be tightly integrated with the lakehouse and Unity Catalog governance, enabling real-time serving, instant branching, and streamlined application development without separate legacy systems.

items.title: Built on object storage, served from cache
items.summary: On November 17, 2026, Databricks Engineering published an overview detailing how Lakebase Postgres achieves high performance while relying on object storage for durability, branching, and transactional and analytical processing (LTAP). While object storage pr…
items.fullStory:
On November 17, 2026, Databricks Engineering published an overview detailing how Lakebase Postgres achieves high performance while relying on object storage for durability, branching, and transactional and analytical processing (LTAP). While object storage provides bottomless storage and instant restores, Carlota Soto noted that reading directly from it can introduce high latency. To counter this, the architecture uses a tiered caching strategy where object storage is kept off the critical read path for active workloads.

Production statistics from Databricks' fleet demonstrate the efficacy of this caching model. The compute node's local cache serves approximately 1.1 billion page accesses per second, accounting for 99.46% of total reads at memory-level latency. When local misses occur, requests move to a pageserver backed by local NVMe, handling about 6 million reads per second (0.54%). Only about 39 requests per second—roughly 1 in every 28 million page accesses, or over 99.99999%—ever reach object storage.

These rare object-storage reads typically occur under specific circumstances, such as accessing old historical branches, performing point-in-time restores, or waking up databases that have been idle for weeks. Once fetched, the data is immediately cached in the faster tiers. Furthermore, pageservers organize data into image layers and delta layers, with p90 metrics staying under 1 delta per GetPage read, ensuring that even off-compute reads avoid heavy replay chains.

The lakebase architecture decouples standard Postgres compute from a storage layer composed of safekeepers for WAL replication, pageservers for managing local NVMe and LSM trees, and object storage for long-term history. Next steps for the platform involve continuing to leverage this decoupled model to provide the cost and durability benefits of object storage without sacrificing traditional database performance.
items.whyItMatters: This architecture proves that Postgres can be successfully built on top of object storage without suffering from latency penalties, achieving over 99.99999% cache-hit efficiency. It redefines how cloud-native databases can combine bottomless storage with high-performance operational workloads.
items.whoIsAffected: Data architects, database administrators, and engineers building applications on Lakebase Postgres.
